paragraphs: Learning from sequences requires handling relationships between events that may be far apart. But determining whether such relationships exist in data, and whether a trained network represents them, is itself a measurement problem. This paper addresses that problem for deep sequence modeling, with language and music as its stated subject.

The authors build a statistical framework around the theory of stochastic processes with long memory. Rather than relying only on heuristic indicators of distant dependencies, they use this theory to formulate implications that can be tested. The central comparison is between long memory in a data source and the way that memory appears in a learned representation.

They investigate these implications through a semiparametric approach adapted to high-dimensional settings. This provides a way to study the relationship between sequence structure and neural representations within a statistical framework. The contribution is a method for asking and testing more precise questions about long-range dependence, rather than a stated finding that particular architectures always preserve or lose it.
icml-2019-a-statistical-investigation-of.tldr: The paper develops a statistical framework for testing how long-range dependence in sequence data is reflected in learned neural representations.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to place sensors adaptively along an interval when events occur randomly and their frequency can vary by location. A placement reveals only part of what happened, so the learner must use incomplete observations to improve subsequent decisions. The available positions form a continuous space rather than a fixed list.

The authors formulate this as a continuum-armed bandit problem, with events modeled by an inhomogeneous Poisson process. Their method combines Thompson sampling with Bayesian histograms that become more detailed over time. These histograms provide a nonparametric way to learn spatial event patterns while the sampling procedure guides action selection under uncertainty.

The paper derives a Bayesian regret bound of order T to the two-thirds power, up to logarithmic factors, over T rounds. It also supplies a polynomial-time procedure for selecting actions. Together, these results address both learning quality and computational practicality. In simulations, the method has substantially lower regret, with less variability, than the competing algorithms tested.
icml-2019-adaptive-sensor-placement-for-.tldr: An adaptive sensor-placement method combines Thompson sampling with increasingly detailed spatial models, supported by a regret bound and favorable simulations.

paragraphs: Planning in reinforcement learning often uses an explicit model of the environment together with a search procedure. Other approaches build planning-oriented structures directly into a neural network. This paper asks whether an agent trained entirely through model-free reinforcement learning can show planning-like behavior using standard components such as convolutional networks and LSTMs.

The authors evaluate planning through several observable capabilities: generalization across a combinatorial state space with irreversible actions, efficient use of training data, and the ability to benefit from additional thinking time. These criteria examine how the agent behaves when solving difficult problems, rather than identifying planning solely by the presence of a particular architecture.

Their experiments find many characteristics associated with planning algorithms. The agent exceeds the reported state of the art in challenging combinatorial domains including Sokoban, and beats other model-free approaches with strong planning-oriented inductive biases. These are empirical demonstrations that ordinary neural components can learn substantial planning-like capabilities; they do not establish that every model-free agent will develop them.
icml-2019-an-investigation-of-model-free.tldr: A model-free agent built from standard neural components empirically exhibits several planning-like capabilities and strong performance on combinatorial tasks.

paragraphs: Stochastic simulators can generate observations even when their likelihoods are too difficult to evaluate for Bayesian inference. One approach learns a posterior distribution from simulations using a neural conditional density estimator. The challenge is that simulations may be generated from proposals that change as inference progresses, and the posterior estimate must account for those choices.

Automatic Posterior Transformation, or APT, is a sequential neural posterior estimation method designed to handle that changing simulation process. It can modify the posterior estimate for arbitrary, dynamically updated proposal distributions. It is also compatible with flow-based density estimators, allowing proposal flexibility to be paired with expressive models of probability distributions.

The authors present APT as more flexible, scalable, and efficient than previous simulation-based inference techniques. Its stated capabilities include working directly with high-dimensional time series and images. This matters because the inference method can accommodate both complex observations and adaptive simulation choices, expanding the kinds of simulator-based problems to which likelihood-free inference can be applied.
icml-2019-automatic-posterior-transforma.tldr: APT enables sequential Bayesian inference from simulators using arbitrary changing proposals and expressive neural density estimators.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a policy would perform using previously collected experience. This paper takes a model-based approach to that task in a batch setting. Instead of relying on a single environment model, it combines parametric and nonparametric models, allowing different models to contribute where their predictions are most useful.

The method first estimates each model's local accuracy. A planner then decides which model to use at each time step, aiming to minimize estimated error in the return over an entire trajectory. This distinction matters: the objective concerns the eventual value estimate, so model selection considers a sequence of decisions rather than treating every prediction as an isolated choice.

The resulting mixture-of-experts approach is designed to achieve the least expected error in its final value estimate. Across the domains evaluated, it outperforms both individual models used alone and state-of-the-art importance-sampling estimators. The findings support selecting among complementary environment models according to their estimated contribution to trajectory-level evaluation error.
icml-2019-combining-parametric-and-nonpa.tldr: A planner combines parametric and nonparametric environment models to reduce estimated trajectory-level error in off-policy evaluation.

paragraphs: A counterfactual visual explanation asks how an image could change to make a vision system favor a specified alternative class. This paper turns that question into a comparison between image regions. The explanation is tied to a particular contrast, helping show what separates the current prediction from the requested alternative.

The method chooses a distractor image that the system assigns to the alternative class. It then identifies regions in the original and distractor images such that replacing the former with the latter would push the prediction toward that alternative. The stated operation encourages the new classification; it is not described as guaranteeing a complete prediction change in every case.

Across multiple image-classification datasets, qualitative results illustrate explanations that are interpretable and distinguish between classes. The authors also test whether these explanations help people learn fine-grained bird classification. Users receiving counterfactual explanations alongside training examples perform better than those learning from the examples alone, showing a concrete teaching benefit in the studied task.
icml-2019-counterfactual-visual-explanat.tldr: Region replacements explain how an image could favor another class and help users learn bird-species distinctions in teaching experiments.

paragraphs: Importance-sampling weights help reinforcement-learning algorithms account for differences between policies. Algorithms such as PPO clip these weights to control variance, but the paper identifies a cost: clipping can introduce substantial bias when actions have many dimensions. It can also make older samples with large weights difficult to reuse effectively.

The proposed improvement clips the importance-sampling weight separately for each action dimension. It also adapts the weight control to bound the policy update relative to the current policy. The aim is to retain the stabilizing role of clipping while avoiding the large bias associated with the usual treatment of high-dimensional actions.

This adjustment enables learning on high-dimensional action tasks and reuse of older samples in a manner resembling off-policy learning. Reusing experience is central to the claimed improvement in sample efficiency, because previously collected interactions remain useful for training. Numerical experiments on various OpenAI Gym tasks show the resulting algorithm outperforming PPO and other reinforcement-learning algorithms included in the comparison.
icml-2019-dimension-wise-importance-samp.tldr: Clipping importance weights separately by action dimension improves PPO-style learning and enables more effective reuse of old samples.

paragraphs: Forecasting a target from several time-varying variables raises two linked questions: what will happen next, and which variables and times contributed to that prediction? This paper modifies an LSTM to address both. Its setting includes a target variable together with exogenous variables that provide additional information for prediction.

The network learns hidden states organized by variable, with the aim of preserving distinct dynamics and separating variables' contributions. A mixture attention mechanism uses those states to model how the target is generated. Associated training methods jointly learn the network parameters and the importance of variables and time points for predicting the target.

Experiments on real datasets show enhanced predictive performance from capturing the dynamics of different variables. The authors also assess the interpretations both qualitatively and quantitatively. The resulting framework brings forecasting and interpretation into the same training process, rather than treating explanatory information as a separate output unrelated to the model's internal organization. The paper presents this as a promising route to forecasting and knowledge extraction.
icml-2019-exploring-interpretable-lstm-n.tldr: Variable-specific LSTM states and mixture attention jointly support forecasting and estimates of which variables and times matter.

paragraphs: This paper develops a common framework for generalized multinomial models used with ranking data. It includes the Plackett–Luce and Bradley–Terry models as special cases, bringing these established models into one treatment. The computational goal is to find the maximum likelihood estimate: the model parameters that best fit the observed data according to likelihood.

The key theoretical result connects that estimate uniquely to the stationary distribution of an inhomogeneous Markov chain. This converts the estimation problem into one with a useful Markov-chain interpretation. The authors use the connection to construct an iterative algorithm that they describe as straightforward to implement and interpret, with guaranteed convergence.

Experiments using synthetic and real data show advantages over existing algorithms: the proposed method reaches the maximum likelihood estimate in fewer iterations and at a faster convergence rate. The framework is readily applicable to page-ranking and sports-ranking problems. Its contribution combines a theoretical characterization of the estimator with a practical procedure for computing it more efficiently in the reported experiments.
icml-2019-fast-algorithm-for-generalized.tldr: A Markov-chain characterization of ranking-model estimates yields a convergent iterative algorithm with faster convergence in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Graphs represent relationships, but their discrete and combinatorial structure makes learning useful representations statistically and computationally challenging. Graphite addresses this by learning node representations without supervision through a deep generative model. The aim is to connect useful representations of individual nodes with a model of the surrounding graph structure.

The framework uses graph neural networks to parameterize a variational autoencoder. Its decoding procedure repeatedly refines the graph, following a strategy inspired by low-rank approximations. This iterative reconstruction is a central architectural contribution: generating graph structure is treated as a refinement process within the latent-variable model.

Across varied synthetic and benchmark datasets, Graphite outperforms competing methods on density estimation, link prediction, and node classification. These tasks examine both modeling graph data and using the learned representations for predictions. The paper also establishes a theoretical connection between graph-neural-network message passing and mean-field variational inference, linking a neural computation used on graphs to a probabilistic inference procedure.
icml-2019-graphite-iterative-generative-.tldr: Graphite combines graph neural networks with iterative generative decoding to learn node representations and improve several graph tasks.

paragraphs: Controlling a team becomes harder when the number of agents changes both during an episode and between episodes. This paper addresses that setting in spatial grid worlds, where flexible control must coexist with collaboration. Its key design choice is to organize the policy around locations in the world rather than a fixed roster of agents.

A convolutional encoder-decoder processes the state as a grid feature map and produces actions for grid locations. Each agent takes the action assigned to its occupied location. Although agents receive actions individually, the network learns a joint spatial representation, and stacked convolutional layers provide a broad receptive field that promotes communication through shared spatial information.

The same convolutional parameters are shared across space, allowing experience discovered by one agent to transfer immediately to others and supporting parallel exploration. The architecture can be integrated with general reinforcement-learning methods, including PPO and Q-learning. Extensive experiments on challenging StarCraft II multi-agent tasks demonstrate its effectiveness, supporting this spatial organization as a way to combine variable team sizes with coordinated behavior.
icml-2019-grid-wise-control-for-multi-ag.tldr: A shared grid-based policy controls changing numbers of agents while using joint spatial features to support collaboration.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether word embeddings contain information about why individual words seem funny. Its scope is single-word humor, and its main finding is that several aspects of such humor correlate with simple linear directions in the vector representations. This makes some humor-related patterns accessible through relatively simple operations on embeddings.

The authors find that the vectors capture multiple features discussed in humor theories from different disciplines. They also represent an individual's humor preferences with a vector that can predict differences in reactions to new, unrated words. Clustering ratings from demographic groups reveals differing humor preferences across those groups.

The study draws on an existing collection of humor ratings and an original crowdsourcing study covering 120,000 words. Its dataset also includes annotations for the theoretically motivated humor features identified by the authors. Together, the results connect embedding structure with both shared humor features and variation between people. The claims concern correlations and predictive patterns in word ratings, rather than a general explanation of all forms of humor.
icml-2019-humor-in-word-embeddings-cocka.tldr: Simple directions in word embeddings correlate with single-word humor and help predict differences in individual humor preferences.

paragraphs: IMEXnet addresses two challenges in convolutional networks: sensitivity to small input changes and the limited spatial reach of convolution operators. The architecture draws on semi-implicit methods for partial differential equations. It adapts that numerical approach to change how information propagates through a deep network.

Compared with similar explicit architectures, including residual networks, the proposed network is more stable. The paper connects this stability to reduced sensitivity to small feature changes and improved generalization. An added implicit step connects every pixel within each image channel, giving the operation access to information across that channel rather than only a limited local region.

The authors state that this broader connectivity remains comparable to standard convolutions in parameter count and computational complexity. That combination matters because the proposed spatial interaction does not require abandoning a convolution-like resource scale. The paper also introduces a semantic-segmentation dataset and demonstrates the architecture's effectiveness using the NYU Depth dataset, linking its numerical design to an image-understanding application.
icml-2019-imexnet-a-forward-stable-deep-.tldr: IMEXnet uses semi-implicit numerical methods to improve network stability and connect pixels across each channel at convolution-comparable cost.

paragraphs: Planning in an unfamiliar environment requires a useful model of how actions affect what happens next. Learning such a model from images is particularly challenging because action selection needs accurate predictions of rewards several steps ahead. This paper introduces PlaNet, a purely model-based agent that learns dynamics from images and plans online in a latent representation.

Its dynamics model combines deterministic and stochastic transition components. The authors also introduce latent overshooting, a variational inference objective that operates over multiple steps. These choices address the need for predictions that remain useful beyond the immediate next transition, where planning depends on consequences that unfold over time.

Using only pixel observations, PlaNet solves continuous-control tasks involving contact dynamics, partial observability, and sparse rewards. The authors describe these tasks as more difficult than those previously solved by planning with learned models. PlaNet requires substantially fewer episodes than strong model-free algorithms while reaching final performance that is close to, and sometimes higher than, theirs. The comparison therefore supports improved experience efficiency without claiming uniformly superior final performance.
icml-2019-learning-latent-dynamics-for-p.tldr: PlaNet learns latent dynamics from images and plans with them, solving challenging control tasks with substantially fewer episodes than strong model-free methods.

paragraphs: Knowledge-graph embedding learns representations of entities and their relationships. This paper highlights a weakness of learning mainly from individual triples: it does not adequately capture longer relational dependencies or propagate semantic information among entities. The authors identify this as especially relevant when representations must connect information across different knowledge graphs.

Their recurrent skipping networks combine recurrent neural networks with residual learning. A skipping mechanism bridges gaps between entities, helping the model capture relational dependencies over longer spans both within and between graphs. The approach builds on the established assumption that similar entities are likely to occupy similar relational roles.

The authors package the networks in an end-to-end framework supporting different tasks. Experiments show better entity-alignment performance than state-of-the-art embedding-based methods and competitive performance on knowledge-graph completion. These outcomes distinguish the strongest reported gain from the broader applicability claim: the method leads the compared alignment approaches, while completion results show that the same framework remains competitive on another graph task.
icml-2019-learning-to-exploit-long-term-.tldr: Recurrent skipping networks capture longer relational dependencies, improving entity alignment while remaining competitive on knowledge-graph completion.

paragraphs: Multigrid methods solve large partial differential equation problems by working across different scales. Their efficiency depends strongly on a prolongation matrix that connects those scales. Because a suitable matrix depends on the problem, designing an effective multigrid method for a new class of equations can be difficult.

This paper learns how to construct that component. A neural network maps discretized equations to prolongation operators for a broad class of two-dimensional diffusion problems. The network is trained once across the whole class using an efficient unsupervised loss, so the learned object is a reusable construction rule rather than an operator fitted separately for each individual equation.

Tests show improved convergence rates compared with the widely used Black-Box multigrid scheme. The authors interpret these results as evidence suggesting that the network learned useful rules for building prolongation matrices. The contribution is therefore a learned component within a numerical solver, with demonstrated benefits for the studied diffusion problems, rather than a claim that one network solves every type of PDE.
icml-2019-learning-to-optimize-multigrid.tldr: A network trained across two-dimensional diffusion problems learns multigrid prolongation operators that improve convergence in reported tests.

paragraphs: Small embedded devices increasingly need to run classification systems, but their memory may be too limited to hold a convolutional network's intermediate activations. This paper treats that storage constraint as the central design problem. The goal is to achieve as much classification accuracy as possible within a strict memory budget.

The proposed memory-optimal direct convolutions trade additional computation for reduced memory requirements. This deliberately explores a different operating point from approaches designed primarily to minimize latency. The motivation is practical: for a device with a hard memory ceiling, an approach that uses more computation can make a useful network fit at all.

The authors validate the technique with an Arduino implementation of ten-class MNIST classification. The network specification, weights, and activations all fit within 2KB of SRAM, while classification accuracy reaches 99.15%. They report this as state-of-the-art accuracy for small-scale embedded systems. The demonstration links the compute-memory trade-off to an actual implementation, with the extra computation remaining an explicit cost of the approach.
icml-2019-memory-optimal-direct-convolut.tldr: Memory-optimal convolutions trade extra computation for storage savings, enabling 99.15% MNIST accuracy with the full network contained in 2KB SRAM.

paragraphs: This paper argues that learning visual representations should include discovering the separate objects in a scene. Instead of treating segmentation as a supervised preprocessing stage, it learns segmentation and object representations together. The starting assumption is simply that a scene contains multiple entities.

Using that structure, the method learns without supervision to divide images into interpretable objects with disentangled representations. It also learns to fill in occluded portions of objects. These capabilities connect identifying an object's visible region with representing aspects of the object beyond what is directly visible in the image.

The reported system extrapolates to scenes containing more objects and to previously unseen objects with new combinations of features. Iterative variational inference also allows it to learn multimodal posterior distributions for ambiguous inputs, so its inferred representation can account for multiple possible interpretations. The approach extends naturally to sequences. Together, these findings show that joint object discovery and representation learning can support several forms of generalization under the paper's multi-entity scene assumption.
icml-2019-multi-object-representation-le.tldr: Iterative variational inference jointly discovers and represents objects without supervision, supporting occlusion completion, ambiguity, and demonstrated generalization.

paragraphs: Separating mixed signals is difficult when training examples are available for only one of the sources. This paper studies a specific version of that problem: a signal from an unobserved distribution is added to a signal from an observed distribution. The goal is to recover the unknown contribution without requiring source examples for both sides.

Neural Egg Separation approaches the task iteratively. It learns to separate the known distribution from increasingly refined estimates of the unknown one. In some settings, the result depends sensitively on initialization, so the authors introduce Latent Mixture Masking to provide a good starting point for the separation process.

Extensive audio and image experiments show that the method outperforms existing approaches using the same level of supervision. It also often reaches performance similar to methods with full supervision. That second result is qualified: comparable fully supervised performance occurs often in the reported experiments, rather than being guaranteed. The contribution is a separation procedure suited to asymmetrical access to source data, with an explicit response to initialization sensitivity.
icml-2019-neural-separation-of-observed-.tldr: Neural Egg Separation iteratively separates additive mixtures when only one source distribution is observed, often approaching fully supervised performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies fair classification through the relationship between fairness and predictability. It expresses that relationship using probability metrics, which provide a way to compare distributions. This places the analysis at the level of distributions and their differences, giving a mathematical language for examining how a repair changes the classification setting.

The authors analyze repair procedures that map conditional distributions to a Wasserstein barycenter. The barycenter serves as a shared distributional destination for those mappings. This makes the repair question concrete: the analysis concerns how conditional distributions are transformed toward that common reference, rather than treating fairness as an unspecified adjustment to a classifier.

The proposed Random Repair is designed to trade minimal information loss against a certain amount of fairness. Its stated contribution is that trade-off, rather than an unconditional promise of perfect fairness while preserving all information. The approach matters because it puts the preservation of information and the amount of fairness into the same repair problem, making both part of the method's objective.
icml-2019-obtaining-fairness-using-optim.tldr: The paper analyzes distributional repairs for fair classification and proposes Random Repair to trade information loss against a degree of fairness.

paragraphs: Curriculum learning changes how training examples are sampled so that mini-batches become progressively more difficult. This paper studies its effects on deep networks, particularly convolutional networks for image recognition. It separates curriculum design into two problems: determining example difficulty and deciding how quickly training should move toward harder examples.

The authors estimate difficulty using either transfer from a competitive teacher network or bootstrapping. They investigate pacing functions to control the progression of sampled batches. Across several architectures and experiments involving CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet subsets, both difficulty-estimation approaches show similar benefits: faster learning and improved final performance on test data.

The paper also provides a theoretical analysis of how curriculum learning changes the optimization landscape. It defines an ideal curriculum and shows that, under mild conditions, this curriculum preserves the corresponding global minimum of the optimization objective. This is a conditional result about the defined ideal curriculum, alongside empirical evidence that practical sampling schedules can improve the training process.
icml-2019-on-the-power-of-curriculum-lea.tldr: Difficulty-based training schedules improve learning in image experiments, while a theoretical ideal curriculum preserves the global minimum under mild conditions.

paragraphs: Batch Bayesian optimization chooses several queries to an expensive black-box function so that their evaluations can run in parallel. This paper argues that a useful batch should combine diversity with good worst-case performance. Choosing a collection of queries therefore requires considering properties of the batch as a whole.

The authors express those priorities in a variational objective. A quantile-based risk measure addresses worst-case performance, while entropy regularization encourages diversity. They then derive a gradient-based algorithm that represents the solution with particles and generalizes Stein variational gradient descent. The optimization procedure is thus tied directly to the two stated goals for batch selection.

The method is evaluated on several real-world applications. The authors report consistent improvements over recent state-of-the-art batch Bayesian optimization methods in those applications, and describe their broader experimental results as better than or comparable to existing methods. These findings support the combined risk-and-diversity objective empirically, without making worst-case optimization performance a universal guarantee.
icml-2019-quantile-stein-variational-gra.tldr: A particle-based batch optimization method balances quantile-based risk and diversity, achieving better or comparable performance in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Black-box adversarial attacks seek image changes that alter a model's prediction without access to its internal workings. The number of queries becomes an important constraint in this setting. This paper proposes a particularly simple attack that assumes the model exposes continuous-valued confidence scores, which provide feedback about the effect of candidate changes.

At each iteration, the algorithm randomly selects a vector from a predefined orthonormal basis and adds or subtracts it from the image. This repeated directional adjustment supports both untargeted attacks and targeted attacks, where a particular alternative prediction is sought. The central contribution is obtaining strong query efficiency from this compact iterative principle.

The authors report previously unprecedented query efficiency in both settings and demonstrate effectiveness in several real-world settings, including the Google Cloud Vision API. They also emphasize fast execution and an implementation requiring fewer than 20 lines of PyTorch. These findings motivate their proposal that the method serve as a strong baseline for future black-box attacks under the stated confidence-score access assumption.
icml-2019-simple-black-box-adversarial-a.tldr: A simple randomized directional attack uses confidence scores to generate targeted and untargeted adversarial images with strong reported query efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper examines how intermediate layers of deep language models use information from input words. Its goal is quantitative explanation: describing the role of word information inside a model in a way that supports consistent interpretation. The focus extends beyond the final prediction to the representations involved in producing it.

The authors define a unified information-based measure to address coherence and generality in existing explanation methods. They report that the resulting explanations remain consistent and faithful across time positions, layers, and different models. A common measure matters here because it provides a shared basis for examining information use across those different parts of a model and across architectures.

The method is applied to four widely used NLP models on three real-world benchmark datasets. The authors use its explanations to account for the models' performances on those tasks. The contribution is therefore an explanatory framework with applications across several models, connecting internal use of word information to observed performance rather than proposing a new predictive architecture.
icml-2019-towards-a-deep-and-unified-und.tldr: A unified information-based measure explains how language models use input words across time positions, layers, and architectures.

paragraphs: Communication between workers can limit the scalability of distributed neural-network training. This paper investigates using redundancy in the training data together with model averaging to reduce that burden. Its target is distributed stochastic optimization for non-convex objectives, where exchanging updates can be a substantial part of the training process.

The authors show theoretically and practically that properly introduced redundancy can reduce the number of communication rounds. Their explanation centers on residual error in local averaging: redundancy reduces this error, allowing the algorithms to reach the same accuracy with fewer rounds than previous approaches. The result depends on using redundancy appropriately, rather than asserting that arbitrary duplication always improves training.

Distributed experiments on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet complement the theoretical analysis. They also reveal additional benefits, including failure tolerance and greater gradient diversity. The work therefore identifies a trade-off in which data redundancy can reduce communication needs, with both an error-based explanation and empirical evidence for useful behavior beyond the reduction in communication rounds.
icml-2019-trading-redundancy-for-communi.tldr: Properly introduced data redundancy reduces local-averaging error, enabling distributed training to reach the same accuracy with fewer communication rounds.
